Retries, duplicate calls and effect identity | "retry idempotency safe method gateway"; "retry idempotency duplicate"; "stock call retry" | tycho.page.43414664520b4866929f7f006f27f59b#3-end-to-end-deadlines-cancellation-and-retry-budgets; tycho.page.d20ce26599b442d2bc00a6e388ac2c35#2-http-method-idempotence-has-a-precise-scope; tycho.page.8d1dbd92ef5042739736443d1f5a3d81#overview |
| F5. Maintained read model versus copy or dual write | "materialized read model CQRS projection"; "read model projection staleness"; "copying data into another service ownership dual write" | tycho.page.5c7d91711de3463eba59be2b16c607e4#overview; tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#3-cqrs-and-asynchronous-projection-freshness; tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes; tycho.page.9daa9ce90a5047fa849c637f24b063f7#1-two-unsafe-dual-write-orders |
| F6. What the composition contract must declare | "composition contract deadlines partial retries"; "gateway aggregation partial response"; "freshness contract stale read version"; "BFF composition ownership" | tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation; tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes; tycho.page.765a54f5d9944577908b40b3fc6cb7ef#1-begin-with-the-authority-and-the-data-contract; tycho.page.6b75e10be102574cdc7351525ebabac9#overview |

## Answer in one paragraph

A database join is one evaluation over one transactional snapshot and one authority. A request-time composition is several independent reads over several authorities at several times, then an in-memory merge; it has no shared snapshot, no distributed transaction and no authority to resolve disagreement, so it cannot be a consistent join in the database sense. It can be a legitimate **reported** view, but only if the report is honest: per-call and whole-request deadlines, an explicit partial-or-fail policy with a versioned shape that marks missing parts, and a retry policy owned at one layer and bounded per dependency and per aggregate. A maintained read model is better when the same shaped query repeats, fan-out latency or partial-failure complexity exceeds the cost of a projection, staleness is tolerable and declarable, and the projection has an owner, a source position, a refresh trigger and a rebuild path. Copying price into the catalogue is not that by default; it is a local replica that becomes a second authority unless it is declared and governed as a projection. The symptoms in the question are contract defects: an empty price block is an undeclared partial result, and a gateway retry of the stock call is an undeclared retry with unbounded fan-out.

## 1. Why the composed response is not a consistent join across owners

A join is a relational operation with one evaluation context: one snapshot, one set of visibility rules, one authority for each predicate, and one transaction boundary that makes the result internally consistent. Composition does not have those properties:

- **The composer calls owners and joins their replies in memory.** API Composition "calls several owner APIs for one request and assembles their responses into a single caller-visible result" (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). Gateway aggregation likewise "composes several owner responses into one client response at the edge" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation). The data is joined after the fact, not inside an owner's transaction.
- **There is no cross-source snapshot.** Per-owner reads happen at different times, so the aggregate can mix owner revisions; a caller's just-committed write may be absent (same API Composition section, the "No snapshot" paragraph). Even a single owner call may read a replica that lags its authority. Version/as-of markers per source, or a read model, are the only ways to make read-your-writes legible; otherwise the page is a collage of different instants.
- **A composition endpoint is not a transaction.** The API Composition owner notes state this explicitly ("a composition endpoint is not a transaction"), and the outbox chapter's failure table states the same structural fact for cross-component work: "There is no atomic transaction spanning all illustrated components" (tycho.page.9daa9ce90a5047fa849c637f24b063f7#1-two-unsafe-dual-write-orders). Composition can read four owners, but it cannot commit, isolate or roll back across them.
- **Strong consistency is a contraindication, not an implementation detail.** The API Composition card rejects the claim "when strong consistency is required" and "when composition needs writes across owners" (tycho.page.ade9759a19a0402594773756d097c11c#overview). Gateway aggregation repeats the boundary: do not aggregate "when strong consistency across owners is required" or when "partial results cannot be represented honestly" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation). If the page's price, stock and availability must agree exactly at one instant, request-time composition cannot deliver that, and no amount of retries or timeouts changes the semantics.

So "consistent join" is the wrong mental model. The composer is a **reader and reporter** of per-owner facts. Its product is an observation with a declared completeness and freshness, not a transaction. That is not a defect if the observation is labelled; it is a defect when the label is missing.

## 2. The two observed symptoms are contract failures, not transport failures

### 2.1 The empty price block is an undeclared partial result

When pricing is slow and the page returns with an empty price block, the composition has made a policy decision silently: it chose "partial response" and encoded it as "no value". Those are different claims. An empty block can be read as free, as not applicable, as unavailable, or as a rendering bug. The API Composition owner notes require the opposite: "One slow or failed participant must not silently disappear from the result; apply per-call deadlines, mark missing parts or fail the composition explicitly" (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). They also record Azure's aggregation guidance: a gateway can "return a partial response when missing data is acceptable, or it might fail the entire request when complete and consistent order data is required", and the team should "Make this decision explicit in the policy design so that clients experience predictable behavior" (same section).

Graceful Degradation supplies the same test from the resilience side: a degraded response is legitimate only when "a degraded response is explicitly less accurate or contains less data; the reduced outcome and the caller-visible state are declared", and it must be rejected "when it silently changes correctness" (tycho.page.f13601692470d89f22c2549bdbb3cd5b#overview). The book goes further: "silent loss of correctness is worse than an explicit failure: each mode needs an entry condition, a visible status, an owner and an audited override" (same card). The optional-dependency walkthrough makes the contrast concrete: on an optional-service timeout, the legitimate action is to "return core success with explicit absent recommendations", while the unsafe row is to "Retry stalled optional call before completing critical booking" (tycho.page.c5d20ae7ef6445e5b23dd5fbac625060#engineering-walkthrough-optional-dependency-failure-creates-core-work-starvation).

The defect is therefore not that the page degraded. The defect is that the page did not say which fields were absent, why, at what freshness, or whether the omission was allowed. An empty price block without a per-field status is a silent contract change.

### 2.2 The gateway retry re-sends the stock call because retry ownership was never declared

A retry is a new attempt at the same logical call, not a fresh request. If the stock call is a pure read, the immediate cost is duplicated work and a second observation that may differ from the first; if it holds, reserves or decrements stock, the retry can create a duplicate effect unless the operation has a stable effect identity and the receiver deduplicates. Gateway Aggregation is explicit: "Fan out in parallel, cap retries per dependency and for the whole aggregate, and expose which dependency failed; a gateway retry must not multiply load across every participant" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation).

The deadline and retry chapter adds the ownership rule: "Retry only at the layer immediately above the layer that rejected the request. Lower layers should return a classified result, not independently retry work that the caller has already judged non-retryable" and "Avoid retry amplification across proxy, API and downstream clients; designate where retries are owned and instrument actual attempt counts" (tycho.page.43414664520b4866929f7f006f27f59b#3-end-to-end-deadlines-cancellation-and-retry-budgets). A gateway retry of a call that the composition already retried, or that a lower client retried, is exactly the amplification the chapter warns about. And retry safety is not established by the HTTP method alone: RFC 9110 makes safe methods idempotent "under intended request effect semantics", but "The method's abstract semantics do not prove a particular handler is correctly implemented, nor that any non-idempotent POST is safe to repeat automatically" (tycho.page.d20ce26599b442d2bc00a6e388ac2c35#2-http-method-idempotence-has-a-precise-scope). If the stock call can change an effect, it needs an application effect key, not a gateway retry.

## 3. When a maintained read model is the better choice

### 3.1 Fit conditions

A maintained read model (a CQRS projection, materialized view or page-shaped derived store) is the better choice when the query shape is repeated and expensive to compose, and when the freshness cost can be stated and accepted:

- **Repeated, shaped reads dominate.** The API Composition owner notes say "a maintained read model may be cheaper for repeated composition" and that filtering, sorting and pagination cannot generally be delegated to owners, so the composer over-fetches and joins in memory (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). A product page is exactly a repeated shaped read: one key, a fixed set of blocks.
- **Fan-out latency or partial-failure complexity exceeds the duplication cost.** The API Composition card's competing alternative is "A maintained read model", and it says to reverse the choice "when composition latency and partial-failure complexity exceed the duplication alternative" (tycho.page.ade9759a19a0402594773756d097c11c#overview). The owner notes add the selection rule: "prefer composition when the sources are authoritative and the caller needs a live view" (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes).
- **Staleness is acceptable and declarable.** CQRS fits when "Read and write workloads differ; projections can be asynchronous; stale reads are acceptable; duplicate/order handling is owned" and "the write model remains the only authority for command-owned state" (tycho.page.5c7d91711de3463eba59be2b16c607e4#overview). If the journey cannot tolerate lag and cannot wait for a version, the authority read path is the alternative.
- **The projection has an owner and a rebuild path.** CQRS is rejected "when every read requires immediate consistency with no version-wait or authority-read path, or when projection maintenance has no owner" (same card). A read model without an owner is not a design; it is an orphaned copy.

### 3.2 What the read model must carry, and what it costs

A read model is derived data, not a new authority. The owner page requires that "A materialized view must record its source version or offset, refresh trigger and freshness contract. A stale view is a derived read, not authority; a query that requires current state must use an authority path" (tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#3-cqrs-and-asynchronous-projection-freshness). The write side keeps command authority: "The write model owns command authority and the read model is a derived, read-only view; neither side may claim authority merely because it can read the other's tables" (tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes).

The costs are real and belong in the decision: projection lag, duplicate apply, cursor gaps, schema drift and rebuild duration are normal failure modes; the apply must be idempotent, the derived row and cursor committed atomically, and rebuilds run with outbound side effects disabled (CQRS card and owner page). A projection that cannot be rebuilt from the authority "is a second database without an owner" (materialized-view notes in the same bounded section). The read contract must publish "the position it has applied and the staleness callers should expect", not leave freshness in an operator's memory (CQRS Read Projections notes, same section). Freshness should be measured as projection age and offset gap, with an approved requirement and representative tests, not asserted as a number (tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#3-cqrs-and-asynchronous-projection-freshness).

So the read model is better when all of the following hold: the page query repeats; the fan-out is the latency or failure bottleneck; partials are hard to represent honestly at request time; a bounded staleness is acceptable per field; and a team owns the projection, its position, its refresh and its rebuild. It is worse when every read needs immediate consistency, when the query shape changes constantly, or when the projection would be a copy nobody maintains.

### 3.3 Why copying price into the catalogue is not the same thing

The proposal "copy price data into the catalogue service so the fan-out disappears" removes one call but does not, by itself, produce a read model. A local copy of another owner's fact is a replica: "When a command needs facts owned by another service, a local replica is a cache of that owner's state, not a second authority. Give it an owner, a source version, refresh/invalidation and reconciliation when the owner changes; the local copy must never become the decision-time writer" (tycho.page.7beb6ba382a1458dbfba5800ff1b53af#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). Without those properties, the catalogue becomes a second price authority: price changes now have two write paths and no atomic transaction across them. The outbox chapter shows the two unsafe orders: write the local store then publish and crash, or publish then fail to commit, leaving a claimed change that never happened (tycho.page.9daa9ce90a5047fa849c637f24b063f7#1-two-unsafe-dual-write-orders). That is not a join fix; it is a consistency problem moved into the catalogue's schema.

Two further points follow. First, copying only price does not remove the page fan-out: catalogue, stock and review reads remain, so the composition still has several owners, partial-failure policy and deadlines. If the goal is to remove the fan-out, the unit to materialize is the **page-shaped read model** across the participating owners, with each source's version and freshness, not one field inside another owner's domain store. Second, a price copy can be legitimate if it is explicitly a cache or projection: owned by the catalogue or page team, with a source version, invalidation on price change, reconciliation, a declared staleness bound and an authority fallback for decisions that need current price. That is a read model with a narrow scope, not an ownership transfer.

### 3.4 The composing layer may be a BFF, but that does not make it an authority

If the composition is a Backend for Frontend, the BFF is a legitimate owner of a client-specific composition: it "composes several owner APIs for one client experience", and the pattern fits when "a team can own each BFF", "shared domain services remain authoritative" and "duplicated client-specific composition is acceptable" (tycho.page.6b75e10be102574cdc7351525ebabac9#overview). It is rejected "when BFFs would duplicate domain logic" or "when no team owns a BFF lifecycle". The BFF card also names the maintenance risk: independent BFF and domain lifecycles create release-alignment risk, so the team should "treat BFF/domain divergence as drift, version the composition and test the client contract" (same card). A BFF therefore changes **who owns the composition**, not whether the response is a consistent join; it still needs the deadline, partial-result and retry declarations in section 4, and it must not become a second domain authority.

## 4. What the composition contract must declare

The contract is the artifact that turns an ad-hoc fan-out into an operable interface. It must declare at least the following.

### 4.1 Deadlines

- **One end-to-end budget, fixed at ingress.** "A timeout on one socket is not a complete request deadline. The caller has an end-to-end business time budget; proxies, authentication, queueing, internal RPCs and durable state can consume it" (tycho.page.43414664520b4866929f7f006f27f59b#3-end-to-end-deadlines-cancellation-and-retry-budgets). The contract should state the page budget, the per-source allocation and the margin, not four independent timeouts.
- **Propagate the remaining budget, not a fresh timeout.** "Each hop should use at most the remaining deadline, minus its own processing and margin, and propagate the remainder" (tycho.page.43414664520b4866929f7f006f27f59b#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). A relative duration with elapsed time deducted avoids wall-clock skew; the Deadline Propagation card adds that "each hop enforces expiry before more work" and that expiration must be observable (tycho.page.364e2c08af2a47249d9d3431346f046c#overview).
- **Enforcement and missing-deadline behavior.** "Requiring a deadline at ingress, rejecting a missing propagated deadline on bounded paths, and moving cleanup to durable work are Tycho guidance" (bounded notes). A propagated value without an enforcement point "is only a hint", and an omitted timeout header can mean an infinite timeout, silently removing the bound (Deadline Propagation card). The contract must say which is mandatory.
- **Timeout ownership and unit.** "Name the timeout owner, the unit (connect, read, total) and the retry interaction; a timeout that silently becomes a retry can multiply load. The timeout value must be observable" (bounded notes). This is precisely the stock-call failure in the question.
- **What survives the deadline.** "An API must define which result is still meaningful after the caller stops waiting, and what resource cleanup follows" (deadline section). Cancellation stops work where possible but "is not proof that a previously committed effect was undone" (same section); cleanup and reconciliation need a durable workflow, not an unbounded request task.

### 4.2 Partial results

- **Required versus optional per source, per query shape.** The contract must say which blocks may be absent and which make the page invalid. Graceful Degradation requires that "Essential and optional work are distinguishable" and that "the reduced outcome and the caller-visible state are declared" (tycho.page.f13601692470d89f22c2549bdbb3cd5b#overview). If price is essential or contractual, the honest response is an explicit failure, not an empty block.
- **Partial-or-fail policy, explicit and predictable.** The API Composition notes cite Azure's choice between "a partial response when missing data is acceptable" and failing "the entire request when complete and consistent order data is required", and require the team to "Make this decision explicit in the policy design so that clients experience predictable behavior" (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). The policy belongs in the contract, not in an exception handler.
- **A versioned shape that marks missing parts.** "A partial response needs a versioned shape that marks missing parts rather than silently omitting them" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation). Each block needs a status that distinguishes unavailable from not-applicable from genuinely empty or zero, plus the source version or as-of time observed. "Expose which dependency failed" is part of the same contract sentence.
- **Freshness and read-your-writes.** A composed page mixes revisions; the contract should carry per-source version/as-of markers so a caller can tell what it is looking at, or route read-your-writes journeys to a version-wait or authority read (API Composition notes). For a read model, publish the applied position and expected staleness in the read contract (CQRS Read Projections notes).
- **Visible degraded state and its owner.** Graceful Degradation requires "a visible status, an owner and an audited override" plus an entry condition and recovery hysteresis (tycho.page.f13601692470d89f22c2549bdbb3cd5b#overview). A degraded page without a status is indistinguishable from a correct page.
- **Bounded join work.** The composer must bound over-fetch, memory and merged-page stability; filtering, sorting and pagination cannot generally be delegated, so the contract should state the ordering and page-stability rule (API Composition notes, "Query shape").

### 4.3 Retries

- **One retry owner.** "Retry only at the layer immediately above the layer that rejected the request" and "designate where retries are owned and instrument actual attempt counts" (tycho.page.43414664520b4866929f7f006f27f59b#3-end-to-end-deadlines-cancellation-and-retry-budgets). If the gateway retries, the composition must not also retry the same call; if the composition retries, the gateway must return a classified result instead.
- **Retryable classes only.** "Retry only a documented retryable failure class, with a bounded total deadline and bounded attempt/backoff budget; observe server pushback/backpressure" (same section). Permanent failures, broad overload and a deadline that cannot fit another attempt are not retryable; a backend should propagate a specific "overloaded; do not retry" signal rather than a generic error (same section).
- **Effect identity before transport retries.** "First ask whether the operation is read-only, semantically idempotent, or protected by an application effect key" (same section). HTTP method semantics are not proof; a command needs an idempotency identity that binds one logical intent, caller/payload scope and retention to an authoritative outcome record (tycho.page.8d28a6e14a1c49d6b67bf9cb5bfb242f#integrated-decision-and-reading-route, and tycho.page.d20ce26599b442d2bc00a6e388ac2c35#2-http-method-idempotence-has-a-precise-scope). If the stock call has an effect, the contract must say so and require the key; if it is read-only, the contract must say that the retry is safe but still bounded.
- **Budgets and the deadline.** "Every attempt must consume the same end-to-end deadline and attempt budget, so added delay cannot extend the caller's useful completion window" (deadline bounded notes, Retry with Jitter). The contract needs an attempt cap, backoff with jitter, a per-dependency cap, a whole-aggregate cap and a service-wide retry budget; "The policy needs an owner and a visible attempt metric; an exponential curve without a deadline check can spend the caller's budget after the result stopped being useful" (same notes, Retry with Exponential Backoff). Gateway Aggregation states the aggregate rule directly: "cap retries per dependency and for the whole aggregate" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation).
- **Ambiguous outcomes.** "Prefer explicit outcome lookup for an ambiguous durable command, rather than treating every timeout as 'nothing happened'" (deadline section). A timeout after commit is not a non-event, and a retry that assumes otherwise can duplicate it.

### 4.4 Cross-cutting declarations

- **Version the composition and each owner adapter.** "The composition endpoint and each owner adapter need an explicit version and a propagated trace context, because a composed failure spans several calls" (tycho.page.cccbd188936543a2aaf904f4002236d8#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes). Gateway Aggregation adds per-call authorization: "Each downstream call carries its own deadline and authorization" (tycho.page.99c509e133d9494fbb3080b6212b7ba7#gateway-aggregation).
- **Declare authority and freshness per field.** The cache authority table asks, for each value, "Which system/state revision determines the correct value?" and "Maximum tolerated age/version gap for the user journey" (tycho.page.765a54f5d9944577908b40b3fc6cb7ef#1-begin-with-the-authority-and-the-data-contract). A page with a price block, a stock block and a review block has at least three such answers.
- **Name the composition owner and test it.** API Composition fits when "composition logic is owned and tested" (tycho.page.ade9759a19a0402594773756d097c11c#overview). The contract without an owner is documentation, not an interface.

## 5. Decision rule and boundaries

Use request-time composition when the page is read-mostly, the shape is small and stable, per-owner calls can carry bounded deadlines, partial results and their failure behavior can be represented, the composition logic is owned and tested, and the response does not require a distributed transaction (tycho.page.ade9759a19a0402594773756d097c11c#overview). Prefer it when the sources are authoritative and the caller needs a live view (API Composition notes).

Use a maintained read model when the same page query repeats, the fan-out latency or partial-failure complexity exceeds the cost of a projection, filtering/sorting/pagination across owners is required, staleness is acceptable and declarable, and a team owns the projection, its source position, refresh trigger, freshness contract and rebuild path (API Composition card; CQRS card and owner page). Do not use one when every read requires immediate consistency with no version-wait or authority-read path, or when projection maintenance has no owner (CQRS card).

Do not silently return an empty block when a source is slow. If the block is essential, fail the composition explicitly; if it is optional, mark it absent in a versioned shape and expose the failed dependency and the degradation state. Do not let a gateway retry multiply the fan-out; assign one retry owner, bound attempts per dependency and per aggregate, and check effect identity before repeating a call. And do not call a copy a read model: a copy becomes acceptable only when it has an owner, a source version, refresh/invalidation, reconciliation, a declared staleness bound and an authority fallback, and never becomes the decision-time writer.

## 7. Unknowns and limits

- **No production evidence.** Every mechanism above is a pattern or design rule. The book explicitly labels the 900-ms budget as hypothetical and the pattern pages as living documents, not benchmarks. This answer does not claim any measured latency, error rate or cost.
- **No numeric budgets are given.** The question does not state the page budget, the price-service latency distribution, price volatility or the tolerated staleness. The contract must set these from an approved requirement and representative tests; the book warns against claiming a freshness threshold without both.
- **The stock call's semantics are unknown.** The question says "a gateway retry re-sends the stock call" but not whether the call reads stock or holds/reserves it. If it has an effect, the retry needs an application effect key; if it is a pure read, it still needs a retry cap and an observation-freshness marker. This distinction changes the contract but not the recommendation to declare it.
- **The essential/optional classification is a product decision.** The sources say a degraded response must be declared, but they do not say whether price, stock or reviews are essential for this page. If price is contractually required, the honest policy is fail-whole-request; the answer cannot choose that for the owner.
- **The composition owner is unnamed.** The question does not say whether the composing layer is a gateway, a BFF or a dedicated composition service. The contract requirements are the same, but the retry owner and the versioning point differ.
- **HTTP status encoding is not specified by the evidence.** The sources require a versioned shape that marks missing parts; they do not prescribe whether that is a distinct status code or an in-body status. The contract should choose one and document it; this answer does not invent one.
- **A read model's freshness bound and rebuild cost are unverified here.** The CQRS pages describe what must be recorded and measured, not a threshold for this page. The decision needs the owner's staleness requirement and a rebuild test before the read model is accepted.

tasks.question: A team declares its service clean architecture because the diagram has four rings. The domain module imports the ORM and the web framework, a service locator supplies adapters at runtime, and the build checks only that packages compile. The team also adds mappers and ports around a small CRUD module that has one database and no second implementation. Why is the ring count not the mechanism, what does the inward dependency rule actually protect, and what does a passing import check fail to prove?
tasks.answer:
# Q280 — Four rings are a drawing; the dependency rule is the mechanism

## 0. Short answer

The team has a diagram, not a demonstrated architecture. A four-ring picture is a notation for the inward dependency rule; it is not the rule, it does not enforce the rule, and it says nothing about runtime binding. The domain importing the ORM and the web framework is a direct violation of the rule. A service locator can re-bind the domain to an adapter at runtime while the source graph looks clean. A build that only compiles checks type consistency, not dependency direction; even a real static import check proves only source imports, not runtime coupling, data behavior, or organizational decoupling. The inward rule protects the domain's source-level freedom to change and be tested independently of volatile technology details — not transactionality, availability, deployment isolation, or release ownership. Ports and mappers around a small CRUD module with one database and no second implementation are, on those facts, more likely ceremony than architecture: they are justified only by a real substitution, test, or change boundary. The team should replace the ring claim with an enforced dependency policy and behavior tests, and remove abstractions that protect nothing.

## 1. Facet matrix

| Facet | Query formulations | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Ring count versus mechanism | "clean architecture rings dependency rule"; "layer count number of layers"; "layered architecture enforced direction" | D (bounded pattern ownership notes), A (clean/onion card), F (port contract) |
| What the inward rule protects | "dependency inversion stable abstractions"; "domain independent of ORM"; "tests isolate policy from infrastructure" | B (purpose and decision question), A (clean/onion card), C (engineering walkthrough) |
| Enforcement and import checks | "fitness function architectural dependency test"; "enforced dependency test build"; "compiler type checker proves imports" | K (module enforcement), D (bounded notes), H (build/test/runtime scope) |
| Runtime binding and service locator | "service locator"; "static imports runtime dependencies"; "composition root wiring" | D (bounded notes), C (engineering walkthrough), L (static-imports case) |
| CRUD ports and mappers | "ports no second implementation"; "small CRUD mapping overhead"; "abstraction cost exceeds isolation" | A (clean/onion card), D (bounded notes), M (atlas entry inventory), H (build/test/runtime scope) |
| Behavior and acceptance | "fake repository constraints"; "architecture acceptance tests"; "dependency or integration test rejects bypass" | C (engineering walkthrough), I (failure and test matrix) |

## 2. Why the ring count is not the mechanism

### 2.1 A count describes the drawing, not the code

The four rings are a vocabulary: entities, use cases, interface adapters, and frameworks/drivers. The dependency rule says source dependencies point inward. The count is not a constraint on the code; it is a property of the picture. You can draw four rings around a domain that imports the ORM and the web framework, and the count is still four. The picture has not become false; the claim that the picture describes the code has. Tycho's bounded guidance is explicit: "The dependency rule, not the number of drawn rings, is the mechanism." [C1] It also warns that "drawing circles as team boundaries is not sufficient" [C1], and it makes the same geometric point for the hexagon: "The geometric term *hexagon* is not a requirement to have exactly six sides or six ports." [C1] The same applies to four rings: the geometry is a metaphor, not a causal mechanism.

### 2.2 The mechanism is an enforced dependency policy

The mechanism has four parts, none of which is the ring count:

1. A declared allowed direction: presentation may call application, application may call domain, and the domain calls neither. [C2]
2. Ports or interfaces declared on the inner side, with adapter implementations outside. [C4]
3. Enforcement in build/dependency tests: the rule is "enforced by build/dependency tests, not by a diagram"; "Put that rule in build checks, not only in a diagram." [C2]
4. Named public surfaces and bypass tests: the owner of each layer names its public surface and the test that catches a bypass; a pass-through layer or cyclic import is evidence that the layer is not a real boundary. [C12]

A ring count supplies none of these. It does not say which edges are allowed, which packages are public, what fails on violation, or how the runtime is composed. That is why "four rings" can be true while the architecture is false.

### 2.3 The team's own facts falsify the claim

The domain imports the ORM and the web framework. The corpus says: "The inner domain must not depend on a UI, database or transport adapter." [C3] "No domain module may import a framework, transport or storage dependency." [C3] "Domain code must not depend on adapter or technology types; dependencies point inward." [C3] The team's imports are exactly the forbidden edges. The ring count is not merely insufficient evidence; it is contradicted by the code. A diagram cannot rescue a violated dependency rule, and a passing compile cannot either.

### 2.4 More rings can be worse

The count is also not a quality scale. The corpus warns against layers that add "indirection without a real change boundary" [C12] and says to choose ports or a modular monolith "when explicit ports or module ownership add more value than layer count." [C1] The atlas says layer boundaries must correspond to "real change or test boundaries" and rejects layering that "adds ceremony without protecting a real change boundary." [C12] A four-ring diagram can therefore be a symptom of ceremony, not proof of architecture.

## 3. What the inward dependency rule actually protects

### 3.1 The protected object

It protects the domain's source-level independence from volatile details: the domain model's state transitions, invariants, and business language should not be shaped by an HTTP request or a specific ORM record shape. [C4] This is a source-code rule: it constrains which module may name which, not which module calls which at runtime. The rule keeps the domain policy from depending on the UI, database, transport, or framework. [C3] That is the object: the policy and its language, not the number of layers.

### 3.2 What it buys

- **Change localization.** "Application structure determines which source changes can be made without rewriting unrelated business rules, whether storage or interface technologies can be replaced, and which dependencies must be present during a test." [C4]
- **Test isolation.** "Domain rules are the main asset; several delivery mechanisms or frameworks are plausible; dependency direction can be enforced; tests need to isolate policy from infrastructure." [C4]
- **Source-level substitutability.** A port is "a source dependency direction and semantic contract, not automatically a network port." [C4] Adapters translate technology to the contract.
- **A real change/test boundary.** "A useful port expresses a real boundary whose isolation or substitution matters to business rules or testing." [C4]
- **Semantic honesty.** Adapter-specific errors, timeouts, and retries stay at the edge and do not become domain states. [C4]

### 3.3 What it does not buy

The rule is not a runtime, data, deployment, or organizational isolation guarantee:

- **Runtime.** The question is whether invoking the use case blocks on a datastore even if the type dependency is inverted; "Hexagonal code still depends on the *availability* of the external capability." [C5]
- **Data and transactions.** "Ports do not make a multi-resource transaction atomic... adding an interface merely hides the transport." [C5]
- **Deployment.** "Dependency-inversion in source alone does not prove deploy-time isolation." [C5]
- **Organization.** "Compile-time inversion alone does not solve ownership or release coupling." [C5]
- **Behavior.** A fake repository cannot demonstrate concurrent DB constraints, credential scope, connection cancellation, or remote transport semantics. [C13]

### 3.4 The precise boundary test

The rule protects something only when the boundary is real. A layer that only forwards calls, a cyclic import, or shared mutable data crossing the boundary is evidence that the layer is not a real change boundary. [C12] The clean/onion choice should be reversed "when that independence is not the protected boundary, or when the mapper adds no tested change benefit." [C12] So the rule protects a change/test boundary that is worth protecting; it does not protect a layer name.

## 4. What a passing import check fails to prove

### 4.1 Compile-only is not an architecture check

A build that checks only that packages compile proves that each package type-checks against its classpath. If the ORM and web framework are on the domain's classpath, the domain compiles. A compile-only build does not assert that the domain is forbidden from importing them, that the package graph is acyclic, or that module publics and privates are respected. The corpus lists actual enforcement mechanisms: "module-level build packages, language visibility restrictions, dependency analysis, ArchUnit-like architecture tests, or Spring Modulith's verification APIs." [C6] It asks: "Do dependency checks reject forbidden import paths and cycles?" [C6] A compile-only build does not answer that question. It proves type consistency, not dependency direction. The inference is explicit: a passing compile is compatible with the exact violation the team has. [C6]

A build can enforce direction if the build graph makes forbidden edges impossible (module-level packages or language visibility). That is stronger than compiling packages with all dependencies available. The described build is the weaker kind: it checks compilation, not allowed edges. The difference matters: "The rule is enforced by build/dependency tests, not by a diagram." [C2]

### 4.2 Even a real static import check stops at source imports

Suppose the team replaces the compile-only build with a genuine static dependency check (ArchUnit-like or a module graph). It can prove that source imports follow the encoded rules. It still does not prove runtime coupling:

> "A static dependency check proves imports, not runtime coupling: reflection, a service locator or generated wiring can still bind the domain to a framework." [C7]

That single sentence is the center of the question. The check sees the source edge, not the runtime object graph. A domain that calls a locator has a source edge to the locator, not to the ORM; the locator can return an ORM-backed adapter at runtime. The check passes; the domain still executes against the framework. [C8]

### 4.3 The service locator is the named blind spot

The team's service locator is exactly the named bypass. If the domain calls the locator to obtain a repository or gateway, the source dependency is on the locator. The concrete adapter is supplied at runtime. The import check cannot see which adapter is bound, whether it is ORM-backed, or whether the domain receives framework types. The runtime dependency remains: the use case still blocks on the datastore even if the type dependency is inverted. [C8] The locator also hides the concrete dependency from tests and from the source graph; failures move from compile time to startup or runtime. That last sentence is an inference from the named runtime-binding risk, not a source claim; the corpus states the risk, not a full service-locator critique. [C8]

The remedy is not another ring. It is explicit composition-root wiring: construct the adapter outside the domain, pass the port in, and keep the locator out of domain code. If a locator remains, restrict it to the composition root and test what it can return. [C8] This remedy is design guidance, not a source claim; the engineering walkthrough's composition-root row supports the need to wire adapters outside the domain.

### 4.4 The runtime, data, organizational, and behavioral gaps

A passing static check also fails to prove:

- **Runtime dependency.** The use case can still block on the database; "Hexagonal code still depends on the *availability* of the external capability." [C5]
- **Data behavior.** Ports do not make transactions atomic; "adding an interface merely hides the transport." [C5]
- **Deployment.** Source inversion does not prove deploy-time isolation. [C5]
- **Organizational coupling.** Two teams may still have to coordinate contracts, migrations, and deployments. [C5]
- **Real-adapter behavior.** Fake adapters cannot demonstrate DB constraints, concurrency, connection cancellation, or remote semantics. [C13]
- **Fitness.** The check cannot tell whether a boundary protects a real change/test boundary or is a pass-through or ceremony. [C12]
- **Completeness.** It checks only the rules encoded; an unencoded forbidden edge passes. This is an inference from the fact that a check asserts only its encoded rules.
- **Build-version parity.** Tests must run on the actual build versions. [C6]

### 4.5 The reflection case is an existence proof

The corpus records a publisher-reported migration where source-based dependency targets "could not always detect classes loaded by reflection from configuration," and "roughly 100 of about 700 services" failed. [C9] This is not a universal failure rate, and the source says it is "not proof that Bazel generally cannot represent reflective dependencies." [C9] It is an existence proof that source analysis can miss runtime dependencies. The lesson is not "static checks are useless"; it is "a static check proves a source-level property, not the runtime graph." [C7]

### 4.6 What a check can prove

A real static import check can prove that the encoded source rules hold for the analyzed build: allowed edges, no forbidden imports, no cycles, and perhaps public/private visibility. That is valuable. It is necessary but not sufficient. It does not prove the architecture is fit, the runtime is decoupled, the data is safe, or the ports are worth their cost. [C7] [C12]

## 5. The CRUD module: ports and mappers without a second implementation

### 5.1 The evidence-based judgment

On the stated facts — small CRUD, one database, no second implementation — the substitution rationale is absent. The corpus is direct:

- "Reject the claim when mapping overhead dominates a small CRUD application or when ports have no genuinely different implementations; prefer simpler layering then." [C10]
- The atlas rejects "a trivial CRUD surface with one stable adapter; when no domain behavior exists to isolate; when the team cannot own mapping and contract tests." [C10]
- "If the application will always have one simple persistence choice, avoid a hierarchy of adapters that adds indirection without needed substitution." [C10]
- "If there is only one stable adapter, interfaces everywhere may add ceremony rather than useful replaceability." [C10]
- "A layered or modular-monolith structure can be simpler when one persistence choice is stable." [C10]

On those facts, the mappers and ports are speculative indirection, not clean architecture. In plain terms, this is speculative generality: paying for a variation that has not been shown to exist. They do not create a second implementation, they do not remove the database, and they do not by themselves make the domain testable. They add mapping code, DTOs, contract and integration tests, and places where latency and adapter errors can hide. [C10] [C13]

### 5.2 Why the indirection costs

A port is a semantic contract, not a network port. [C11] Around one database, it does not make the transaction atomic or the database disappear; "adding an interface merely hides the transport." [C11] A mapper can hide latency and translate errors inconsistently; the boundary needs contract tests and explicit error translation to stay honest. [C13] If the layer only forwards calls, it is not a real change boundary. [C12] The team pays the mapping cost without a change scenario that the mapping enables. That is the definition of ceremony in this context.

### 5.3 When it would be justified

The abstractions are justified if they protect a real boundary:

- a second implementation, production or a meaningful test adapter;
- a volatile vendor, legacy, or remote boundary;
- domain behavior that needs isolated rule testing;
- staged modernization where the adapter boundary is the seam.

The corpus's good-fit conditions include "several delivery mechanisms or frameworks are plausible," "tests need to isolate policy from infrastructure," and "more than one adapter or technology is plausible." [C4] [C10] A test adapter can be a legitimate second implementation, but a small CRUD module with no domain behavior gives it little to prove; that test-adapter case is an application of the corpus's test-isolation condition, not a separate source claim. The decision test is not "do we have ports?" but "what change or test does this port make possible, and is that benefit tested?" [C12]

### 5.4 Recommendation

Collapse the ports and mappers unless a named boundary pays for them. Keep a thin seam only where a real test, substitution, or change need exists. If the mapper keeps ORM types out of the domain and that is tested, state that as the benefit; otherwise it is ceremony. The team should be able to say which change becomes cheaper and which test becomes possible. If it cannot, the abstraction is not architecture.

## 6. Decision rules for the team

1. Replace the ring claim with a written dependency policy: allowed edges, public surfaces, forbidden packages, and cycles. [C2]
2. Enforce it at the build graph, not only in a diagram: module-level packages or language visibility so the domain cannot compile against the ORM and web framework; add ArchUnit-like tests for forbidden imports and cycles. [C6]
3. Run the checks on the actual build versions, and fail the change. [C6]
4. Add runtime composition tests: start the composition root, assert the domain receives only port types, and test what the service locator can return. [C8]
5. Add real-adapter behavior tests: DB constraints, concurrency, transaction isolation, connection cancellation, and remote failure. Fake adapters alone are not enough. [C13]
6. Remove the service locator from domain code; wire adapters explicitly at the composition root. If the locator stays, confine it to composition and test its bindings. [C8]
7. Remove ports and mappers that protect no real boundary; keep only seams with a named change or test benefit. [C10] [C12]
8. Review the three dependencies separately: source, runtime, and organizational. A green import check answers only the first, and only if it actually checks edges. [C5]

tasks.question: a team patches running production hosts for an urgent library fix and records the change in a ticket, while the next deploy builds a new image from the repository and never compares it with what is running. drift remediation is manual, several hosts keep local state, and rollback means re-running the old patch script. the team says it already uses immutable infrastructure because images are built in ci. why does building images not make the fleet reproducible, what must each instance, image and rollback path record before replacement is safe, and when is configuration management on long-lived hosts the better choice?
tasks.answer:
# A CI image pipeline is not a reproducible fleet

## Short answer

Building an image in CI proves that a candidate artifact was produced from some source revision. It does not prove that any production instance runs that artifact, that the instance's configuration and local state are recorded, that drift is detected, or that the fleet can be rebuilt and rolled back. Those are the four conditions the atlas attaches to immutable infrastructure: images and artifacts versioned and recorded, drift detected and remediated, state externalized, and replacement, rebuild and rollback automated. This team has an urgent in-place patch recorded in a ticket, a next deploy that builds from the repository without comparing what is running, manual drift remediation, several hosts with local state, and a rollback that re-runs the old patch script. That is a mutable, manually reconciled fleet with a CI pipeline in front of it. Calling it immutable because images are built in CI mistakes one release boundary for the operating model.

**Layers used:** book and atlas. The question is about deployment operating models, per-object records and rollback evidence, so the modeling-and-simulation layer is not needed; no model, scenario, run or decision artifact is cited.

The rest of this answer separates the build boundary from fleet identity, states what each image, instance and rollback path must record, and gives the conditions under which configuration management on long-lived hosts is the better choice.

## 2. Mechanism: why building images does not make the fleet reproducible

### 2.1 CI controls one release boundary, not the fleet

The book separates source revision, build execution, artifact identity, promotion and runtime acceptance. A successful pipeline run does not prove that the intended artifact was deployed or that its persisted effects remain correct. The artifact is the subject, not a mutable tag: a signed attestation bound to digest A is not evidence for digest B even if both share an image name. Deployment identity is a separate check from documentation-derived source identity and from release approval.

That separation is exactly what the team has collapsed. "We build images in CI" answers the build boundary. It does not answer which image is running on each host, which configuration revision that host uses, what local state it holds, or whether the previous artifact can be restored. A clean diff or converged resource state does not mean downstream effects, durable writes or API contracts are correct either. A green pipeline is not a fleet inventory.

The distinction can be stated as three different artifacts:

- A **build output**: bytes with a digest, produced from a source revision and a build recipe.
- A **deployment record**: which digest and configuration an authorized controller attempted to apply to a named target.
- A **running instance**: the artifact actually executing, with its configuration, local state, drift and observed runtime acceptance.

The team has the first, a ticket that partially documents the second, and no reliable record of the third. Reproducibility is a property of the third: every running instance must be reproducible from a recorded artifact digest, and drift must be detected rather than tolerated.

### 2.2 Four independent gaps make this fleet non-reproducible

The scenario contains four gaps. Each one is sufficient to break the claim; together they make the next deploy an uncontrolled change.

1. **Artifact gap: the urgent fix may not be in the image at all.** The patch was applied to running hosts and recorded in a ticket. If it was not backported to the repository, the next image built from the repository does not contain it. If it was backported but the running hosts still hold the patched binary, the image and the hosts are different artifacts. Either way, "the image was built" says nothing about whether the fix survives the deploy. The ticket is not an artifact: it can record why the change happened and who approved it, but it does not identify bytes. A rebuilt image can differ from the deployed artifact, and a deployed tag can point to a different digest than the one that passed the gates. Without a digest comparison, the deploy cannot tell whether it is preserving the fix, erasing it, or creating a mixed fleet.

2. **Conformance gap: no one checks what is actually running.** The next deploy never compares the repository image with the running fleet. Manual drift remediation means each correction is another unreviewed mutation. There is no reconciler observing declared versus actual state, no drift owner, and no exception ledger. The fleet can contain hosts patched on different dates, with different local packages, and with the patch applied in different ways. A ticket records one change, not the cumulative state of each host. This is the definition of a snowflake fleet: each host is individually maintained and no artifact fully describes it.

3. **State gap: several hosts keep local state.** An image carries code and configuration, not the durable data, local caches, queues or device state that make a host unique. Replacing such a host is a data migration. Unless the state is externalized, or snapshotted with an owner, a recovery point and a tested restore, replacement either loses data or silently changes behavior. Immutable replacement is contraindicated when in-place state cannot be externalized; replacement is not a backup. A rollback restores an artifact, not necessarily compatible data.

4. **Recovery gap: re-running the old patch script is not a rollback.** A rollback path is a recorded, tested route back to a known artifact and a known data state. Re-running an old patch script assumes the script still applies to the current host, is idempotent, has not been superseded, and that no new-only writes or external effects occurred since. None of those assumptions is recorded. The script may be unavailable, may depend on a package version that has moved, or may reverse the fix while leaving data written by the fixed version. After new-only writes, an image-only rollback can increase failures; the recovery may need a compatible forward repair or an approved restore with explicit loss.

These gaps are independent. A perfect image build does not close the artifact gap if the fix is only on hosts. A perfect patch record does not close the conformance gap if no one compares digests. A perfect digest comparison does not close the state gap if replacement destroys local data. A perfect state snapshot does not close the recovery gap if the old script cannot restore compatibility. That is why "images are built in CI" is not an answer to any of the three questions in the prompt.

### 2.3 Why a reproducible build is not a reproducible fleet

Reproducibility of a build means that equivalent inputs produce comparable bytes under a defined build recipe. It is a property of the artifact, and even it is conditional: the consumer-side gate must check the deployed package digest, builder identity, provenance and trust root, approved source revision and build recipe, dependency constraints, target authorization, and key validity. A reproducible vulnerability is still a vulnerability. More importantly, byte reproducibility does not establish deployment reproducibility. It tells you what a candidate is; it does not tell you what forty hosts are running, with which configuration, against which data.

Fleet reproducibility requires a recorded mapping from each instance to an artifact digest, a configuration revision, an externalized or snapshotted state, and a tested recovery path. That mapping is what the team lacks. The CI pipeline can keep producing good candidates while the fleet drifts further from them.

### 2.4 "Immutable" is an operating property, not a build location

Immutable infrastructure replaces instances from a versioned image or definition instead of mutating running hosts. The atlas lists four good-fit conditions: images and artifacts are versioned and recorded; drift is detected and remediated; state is externalized; replacement, rebuild and rollback are automated. It rejects the pattern when in-place state cannot be externalized, replacement is too slow, drift is invisible, or artifact identity and the rebuild path cannot be tested. The competing alternative is explicitly mutable servers with configuration management, and the choice reverses when replacement cost exceeds the drift and recovery benefit.

The team has a partial version of the first condition: it builds an image, but it does not record which image each instance runs. It does not have detected and remediated drift, externalized state, or automated replacement and rollback. A CI build is compatible with in-place patching; indeed, a CI deploy can erase an in-place patch if no digest comparison prevents it. Immutability is a property of how the fleet is operated, not of where the build runs.

### 2.5 What the ticket can and cannot do

A ticket is a useful audit index. It should link to the patch artifact, the affected instances, the approval, the expiry of any temporary exception, and the rollback plan. It cannot substitute for the image digest, the instance record or the tested rollback. If the fix is urgent, the durable route is to backport it to the repository, build a new image from the patched source, record and deploy that digest, and compare it with every running instance. Until that is possible, the host patch should be recorded as an explicit, expiring drift exception with a named owner and a replacement deadline, not treated as evidence that the fleet is reproducible.

## 3. What each instance, image and rollback path must record before replacement is safe

The three records answer three different questions:

- The **image record** answers: what is this artifact, and can we rebuild or verify it?
- The **instance record** answers: what is actually running here, and how does it differ from the approved artifact?
- The **rollback path record** answers: if replacement fails, how do we get back to a known artifact and a compatible data state without losing more than we authorized?

### 3.1 Image record: identity and rebuildability

At minimum, each image record should contain:

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Content digest (not only a tag) | The digest is the artifact subject. A tag is mutable, and an attestation for digest A is not evidence for digest B. |
| Source revision | Ties the bytes to a reviewed, immutable input. A branch name is not enough. |
| Build recipe, toolchain and dependency revisions | Makes the build reconstructible and exposes differences between rebuilds. |
| Builder identity, provenance, signature and trust root | Separates "built by an approved builder under an approved process" from "someone produced a file". |
| Authorization and target environment | A valid signature is not deployment authorization; the environment and approver must be bound. |
| SBOM with scope, omissions and image-layer coverage | A source-only inventory does not establish the runtime image's component set. |
| Build ancestry and previous artifact/template | Needed to rebuild the previous image and to compare a rebuilt artifact with the deployed one. |
| Test scope and known skipped checks | A green pipeline with skipped checks is not equivalent evidence. |
| Build time and base-image identity | Supports reproducibility checks and vulnerability response. |

The book's record rule is explicit: record input revision, full toolchain and repository source identity, test scope, known skipped checks, output digest, source/target relationships and failed jobs. A consumer-side verification gate should test the deployed package digest, expected builder identity, verified provenance and trust root, approved source revision and build recipe, approved dependency and source constraints, valid authorization for the target environment, and key rotation and expiration policy. The SBOM should identify the target digest, generation tool, scope, component identities, known omissions, and its relationship to the exact release artifact rather than merely the source tree.

Two subtle points matter for this scenario. First, a rebuilt image that no longer matches the deployed artifact turns replacement into an uncontrolled change; record digests and test the rebuild path. Second, the image record must include the previous image and its template or ancestry, because that is the only artifact a rollback can actually restore. "Rebuild from the repository" is not a rollback path unless the previous image can be rebuilt and its digest compared.

### 3.2 Instance record: actual identity and divergence

At minimum, each instance record should contain:

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Actual deployed digest | The only reliable answer to "what is running here?" A tag or a deployment intent is not enough. |
| Configuration revision and payload digest | Configuration is a distributed transition, not a simultaneous switch. Record the revision actually used, not just the intended one. |
| Drift status and approved exceptions | Any difference from the approved artifact must be visible, owned and expiring. |
| Out-of-band patches, their ticket and expiry | The urgent library fix is exactly such a patch. If it is not in the image, the instance record must say so. |
| Local state inventory and owner | Data, caches, queues, secrets and device state that would be lost or changed by replacement. |
| Snapshot or backup identity, recovery point and tested restore | A backup is not a restore result until integrity and application usability are tested. |
| Runtime acceptance evidence | User outcomes, integrity checks, source revision and deployed digest; a ready process is not acceptance. |
| Environment, target and operator responsibility | The same artifact can be safe in one target and unsafe in another. |
| Last verification time and verifier | A record without an observation time is a claim, not evidence. |

The book separates the same concerns at a higher level: record the state writer, ingress, runtime instance, scheduler/control service, deployment mechanism, network path, secrets/identity service, availability zone/host/region and operator responsibility. In a patched fleet, the instance record is where the ticket, the digest, the configuration revision and the local state meet. If it is hand-maintained, it will drift; it should be produced or verified by the deployment and observation path, not reconstructed during an incident.

For the scenario, the patch ticket must be linked from every affected instance record. Each record should state whether the patch is present in the image, present only on the host, or superseded. If the patch is only on the host, the record should carry an approval, an expiry and a replacement plan. That is what turns an invisible mutation into a managed exception.

### 3.3 Rollback path record: recoverability and data compatibility

At minimum, the rollback path record should contain:

| Field | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Previous artifact digest, retained and unchanged | A rollback must restore a known artifact, not a script that may have changed. |
| Rebuild recipe and ancestry for that artifact | If the previous image must be rebuilt, its template and build metadata must exist and be testable. |
| Old/new compatibility matrix | Old binaries must read new persisted state, and old clients and consumers must accept the old contract. |
| Data recovery point, RPO and permissible loss | A restore may lose acknowledged operations; the business must state what loss is allowed. |
| Old route, environment and authority | The old path must still be operational and authorized, not merely remembered. |
| Tested rollback or forward-repair procedure | An untested plan is not a capability. The path must be exercised before exposure. |
| No-return point and named approver | Some writes and external effects are irreversible; the authority to cross that point must be explicit. |
| Reconciliation and audit evidence | Repair is an authorized mutation; duplicates and external effects must be reconciled, not blindly replayed. |

A code rollback is reversible only if older binaries still correctly interpret persisted state produced by newer binaries; external clients and asynchronous consumers still accept the older response or event contract; effects committed during the new release can be reconciled or safely replayed; the old route is still operational and authorized; and the rollback itself does not reintroduce a known security or correctness defect. That is a five-part test, not a script re-run.

The book also makes the sequencing explicit. Before exposure, prove candidate identity, rollback or forward-repair availability, data and read compatibility, representative readiness, downstream capacity, required security policy and measured SLIs. After new-only writes, there is no automatic image-only rollback; the recovery is a compatible forward repair or a restore with approved loss and reconciliation. A restore may lose acknowledged operations if the recovery point predates their commits, so the permissible business loss must be stated in advance.

### 3.4 The replacement gate

Before replacing any instance, the team should be able to answer "yes" to all of the following:

1. The image record is complete, and the digest being deployed is the digest that was tested and approved.
2. The instance record is complete, and its local state is either externalized, snapshotted with a tested restore, or explicitly declared out of scope with an owner who accepts the loss.
3. Every out-of-band patch is either in the image or recorded as an approved, expiring exception.
4. The rollback path is recorded and has been exercised; old readers can handle new writes, or a forward-repair procedure is ready.
5. The no-return point, approver and permissible data loss are named.

If the released digest or the old/new data compatibility is unknown, the correct state is no-go. A green CI run or a synchronized reconciler is not evidence of safety. That is the direct answer to "before replacement is safe": safe replacement is not a property of the image alone; it is a property of the image record, the instance record and the rollback record being complete and mutually consistent.

## 4. When configuration management on long-lived hosts is the better choice

Configuration management on long-lived hosts is the better choice when the host is the unit of state, not the unit of code. The atlas states the trade-off directly: configuration management on long-lived hosts is cheaper when state locality dominates; choose immutable replacement when reproducibility, an automated replacement path and artifact rollback speed matter. The competing alternative is mutable servers with configuration management, and the choice reverses when replacement cost exceeds the drift and recovery benefit.

The concrete conditions are:

- **State locality dominates.** The host holds data, licensed software, hardware-bound state, large caches or device state that cannot be externalized cheaply. Replacing it is a data migration, not an image swap.
- **Replacement is slow or expensive.** Rebuilding and reprovisioning takes longer than the maintenance window, or requires capacity the team does not have. The atlas lists "replacement is too slow" as a contraindication for immutable infrastructure.
- **In-place state cannot be externalized.** The same contraindication applies even if replacement is technically possible; the data would be lost or would diverge.
- **Imperative, one-off changes dominate.** The GitOps card rejects reconciliation when imperative one-off changes dominate or the reconciler is unowned. A controlled configuration-management process may fit such a fleet better than a reconciliation loop nobody owns.
- **Artifact identity or the rebuild path cannot be pinned or tested.** If the team cannot rebuild the previous image or compare digests, immutable replacement is not a safe operating model yet; a configuration-managed host with a tested change procedure may be the more honest choice.
- **Hardware, licensing or on-disk contracts block replacement.** The book notes that a hard device driver or kernel dependency, unsupported legacy licensing, or an immutable on-disk contract can be a genuine contraindication to container-style replacement. These are evidence questions, not stereotypes.

But configuration management is not "keep doing what you are doing, but write it down". To be a legitimate alternative it needs the same discipline the image path needs:

- a versioned desired declaration, not a pile of ad hoc scripts;
- idempotent convergence, so repeated application is safe;
- drift detection with an owner and an exception process;
- an observed revision and snapshot age, because serving an old value is a deliberate policy, not evidence of convergence;
- a tested rollback or forward-repair path, with data compatibility checked;
- an audit trail that links each change to an approval and to the affected hosts.

Infrastructure as code is a versioned declaration plus a change mechanism, not an availability mechanism by itself. A stored declaration is not proof that production matches it. The same is true of a configuration-management repository: it is evidence of intent, not evidence of convergence. The team's current process is not even that; it is manual patching with a ticket. If the team formalizes configuration management for the stateful hosts, it can be the better interim operating model. If it claims immutability, it must first externalize state, automate replacement, record digests, detect drift and test rollback.

The practical decision rule is therefore not "do we build images?" but "can we produce the image record, the instance record and the rollback record, and pass the replacement gate?" If yes, immutable replacement is a credible fit. If no, and state locality dominates, configuration management on the long-lived hosts is the better choice while the state and replacement path are fixed. If neither is true, the correct action is to stop and gather evidence rather than deploy. The book's safe-rollout alternatives make the same point: explicit downtime with a tested restore can be preferable to a staged replacement when a truly incompatible change cannot be staged safely.

## 5. Boundaries and contraindications

- This is an evidence-based architectural answer from the book and pattern atlas, not a production diagnosis. No host, deployment, drift measurement, rebuild or restore was observed or executed for this answer.
- The atlas card is applicable-under-conditions and its coverage is bounded; it is not independent review or owner acceptance. The sources require versioned, recorded artifacts and drift detection, but no source mandates a particular digest format. "Record the digest" is Tycho's concrete record rule, not a universal vendor requirement.
- Immutable replacement is not a backup. Data, secrets and external effects still need lifecycle ownership, and a rollback restores an artifact, not necessarily compatible data.
- Configuration management is not automatically safer. It can hide drift, accumulate stale overrides, and produce a different snowflake per host. It needs the same versioning, observation and rollback evidence; otherwise it is manual patching with a different name.
- Rebuild determinism is not guaranteed. The correct control is to test the rebuild path and compare the rebuilt digest with the deployed digest, not to assume byte equality.
- A rollback may be impossible after irreversible external effects. In that case the honest choice is a forward repair or an approved restore with explicit loss, not a claimed rollback.
- The pattern choice is reversible. If state is externalized and replacement becomes fast and testable, the balance can move toward immutable replacement. If replacement cost rises or state locality increases, the balance can move back toward configuration management.

## 6. Unknowns

The following facts are not established by the scenario or the evidence, and they change the recommendation:

1. Whether the urgent library fix is in the repository and in the next image, or only on the running hosts.
2. Whether the old patch script is idempotent, still available, and tested against the current host state.
3. Whether any new-only writes or external effects occurred after the patch; this determines whether image rollback is safe at all.
4. What local state the several hosts hold, who owns it, and whether it can be externalized or snapshotted with a tested restore.
5. The RTO/RPO and the business-permissible data loss for each stateful host.
6. Whether the build is deterministic enough to rebuild the previous image and compare digests, and whether the rebuild path has ever been exercised.
7. Whether the next deploy compares actual running digests with the approved digest, or only applies a tag.
8. Whether the team has an inventory of running versions, configurations and out-of-band patches, and who owns drift.
9. Whether a configuration-management system already exists and is idempotent, or whether the team would be building one from scratch.
10. Whether the fleet can tolerate the replacement time and capacity cost, or whether in-place maintenance is the only feasible window.

If items 1, 4, 6 and 7 are resolved in the favorable direction — the fix is in the image, state is externalized, the rebuild path is tested and digests are compared — immutable replacement becomes more credible. If items 4, 5 and 10 point the other way, configuration management on the long-lived hosts is the better choice until the state architecture changes.

The first is to make immutable real: backport the patch, rebuild and record the image, compare digests, externalize or snapshot state, automate replacement and test rollback. The second is to make configuration management real on the long-lived hosts: version the desired state, detect and own drift, record observed revisions and test rollback, while planning the state migration.
